text: You'd never guess Denmark has a desert, but it's 40 meters tall, and it's walking.
Up to 18 meters a year, that's almost a cricket pitch.
So how does a green, rainy country grow a desert?
Danes cut down their forests for timber and farmland.
By 1800, only 2-4% of Denmark was still forest.
So what were those trees doing? Holding the sand down. So the wind took over,
burying farms and whole villages up to seven kilometers inland. Then the sand
reached Skyen's church, the biggest in the region. For 20 years people dug the
door free. Just to get to church. Knock-knock. I'm a church! Show some
was. In 1795, the king closed it. Only the tower still pokes out. So Denmark fought back
with trees, and by the 1950s, the sand was tamed. So why is one dune still walking?
Because Denmark kept it. On purpose! The state bought Roeburg-Mehle in 1900 and lets it
roam free, as a reminder. And the twist? The story goes, the sand that buried that church
came from this very dune. In a century or two, it should reach the main road to Skyen.
